intro: Pemberton sits among the karri forests of Western Australia's wet southwest, and we map four of its karris. Two are climbing trees: the Gloucester Tree, a fire lookout pegged in 1947 with steel pegs a prince helped drill, reopened to climbers in 2026 at a lower platform, and the Dave Evans Bicentennial Tree, pegged in 1988 for climbers, never for fires. A reader found the other two on the back roads west of town: a lone karri on Ritter Road that has swallowed another tree, and two karri stems fused into one base by Anzac Road.
meta_description: The Gloucester Tree in Pemberton, WA: a former fire lookout karri you can still climb via steel pegs, reopened 2026 after a safety closure.
question_meta: Pemberton's four mapped karris: the Gloucester Tree fire lookout, the Dave Evans Bicentennial Tree, and two giants a reader found west of town.
question_answer: Pemberton's oldest mapped tree, the only one of its four with an age on record, is the Gloucester Tree, a Karri (Eucalyptus diversicolor) in Gloucester National Park about 3km from town. Fitted in 1947 with a spiral of steel pegs to serve as a fire lookout, it was once the second tallest such tree in the world, and its climb reopened to the public on 1 July 2026 after a three-year safety closure, now stopping at a lower platform. The other, the Dave Evans Bicentennial Tree about 15km south in Warren National Park, was pegged in 1988 and is closed to climbers until the end of November 2026.
question_context: The tree takes its name from Prince Henry, Duke of Gloucester, who worked an auger into the trunk himself during a visit in the late 1940s. Forester George Reynolds drove the spiral of pegs up the trunk in 1947, one of eight fire-lookout trees raised across the south west between 1937 and 1952, and Jack Watson, a forester and Gallipoli veteran, made the first test climb, taking six hours. At the climbing zone the trunk measured 7.3 metres round on that first ascent. The tree stood 61 metres tall until a trim removed seven metres of rotting crown; the climb closed in November 2023 on safety grounds and reopened in July 2026 at a new platform 37 metres up rather than the old 53. There is no harness and the risk is the climber's own. Its age is given only as a floor, at least 250 years, with no ceiling and no ring count on record. A DPaW day-use entry fee applies for vehicle access to Gloucester National Park; there is no public transport, and Pemberton itself is a short, rural drive away.

faq.a: A karri in Gloucester National Park fitted in 1947 with a spiral of steel pegs as a forestry fire lookout, still climbable today.
At least 250 years, by the sources' own account, with no upper figure and no ring count on record.
Yes. The climb reopened on 1 July 2026 after a three-year safety closure, now stopping at a platform 37 metres up rather than the old 53. There is no harness and the climb is at your own risk.
By car, about 3km (a 5 minute drive) from Pemberton town centre. A DPaW day-use entry fee applies for vehicle entry to Gloucester National Park.

trees.name: The Gloucester Tree

location.address: Gloucester National Park, Pemberton, Western Australia 6260
location.neighbourhood: Gloucester National Park, ~3km from Pemberton town centre

trees.story:
A prince helped drill the holes. Prince Henry, Duke of Gloucester, came through in the late 1940s and worked an auger into this karri's trunk himself, which is how the tree got both its name and part of its ladder.

The ladder was the point. In 1947 the forestry service picked this karri as a fire lookout, one of eight raised across the south west between 1937 and 1952, and George Reynolds drove a spiral of steel pegs up the trunk. Jack Watson, a forester and Gallipoli veteran who later ran Kings Park, made the test climb and took six hours over it. The job at the top was to see smoke over the karri forest before it turned into something visible from the ground. It became the second tallest fire lookout tree in the world, behind the Dave Evans Bicentennial Tree a few kilometres away.

It stood 61 metres until a trim took seven metres of rotting crown off. The climb closed in November 2023 on safety grounds and reopened on 1 July 2026, now stopping at a platform 37 metres up rather than the old 53. There is still no harness and the risk is still the climber's own. At the climbing zone the trunk measured 7.3 metres round on that first ascent in 1947.

Its age is a floor without a ceiling: sources say at least 250 years, and nobody has counted the rings.
trees.access: Free to view; DPaW national park day-use entry fee applies for vehicle entry to Gloucester National Park. Open daylight hours. The climb itself (pegs spiralling the trunk) reopened 1 July 2026 after a 3-year safety closure, now restricted to a new 37m platform (was 53m) after the crown was trimmed 7m for rot; no harness provided, climb at own risk.
trees.transport: No public transport to the park; ~5 minute drive / 3km from Pemberton town, which itself is rural and has limited coach/bus service. Car is the practical way in.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the spiral of steel pegs driven up its trunk to a climbing platform. It stands in Gloucester National Park near Pemberton, Western Australia.

trees.name: Dave Evans Bicentennial Tree

location.address: Old Vasse Road, Warren National Park, near Pemberton WA 6260

trees.access: Warren National Park entry fee applies (day pass or WA parks pass); climbing itself is free. Picnic and barbecue area, toilets and parking. The whole site was closed to 2 October 2026 for re-pegging; it reopens 3 October but the tree stays closed for climbing until the end of November 2026, so confirm with Pemberton Visitor Centre (+61 8 9776 1133).
trees.transport: No public transport; about 15 minutes by car (15 km) south of Pemberton.
trees.story:
This is a lookout tree that never looked out for a fire. The karri lookouts around Pemberton were pegged in the 1930s and 1940s so foresters could spot smoke over the forest. This one was pegged in 1988, for the Australian Bicentenary.

It carries the name of Dave Evans, a local teacher and politician with an interest in tree towers. A spiral of metal pegs runs up the trunk, 165 of them by one count and 130 by another, to a platform about 20 metres up and a hut at the top, above the canopy.

Of the three climbing trees around Pemberton, the Gloucester Tree, the Diamond Tree and this one, it is the tallest. How tall depends on who you ask: 75 metres in one parks listing, 68 in the parks service's Pemberton brochure, 65 on Wikipedia. Nobody has published a girth or an age either, so if you know of one, tell us.

It is in the middle of an overhaul. The pegs and the ladder mesh were renewed in 2026, and the whole site was shut for the work until 2 October. It has reopened, but the tree itself stays closed to climbers until the end of November 2026, so check with the Pemberton Visitor Centre before counting on a climb.

It stands in Warren National Park off Old Vasse Road, about 15 kilometres south of Pemberton by car. A park entry fee applies; the climb costs nothing extra.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the spiral of metal pegs running up its trunk to a hut above the canopy. It stands beside the picnic area off Old Vasse Road in Warren National Park, south of Pemberton.

trees.name: The Karri that Swallowed a Tree

location.address: Verge of Ritter Road, west of Pemberton, Western Australia

trees.how_to_recognise: A lone karri on the grass verge beside a red gravel road, a paddock fence behind it: a hugely thick, dark trunk with a slimmer pale stem standing up inside it into the crown.
trees.access: Seen from Ritter Road, a rural gravel road; the tree stands on the verge in front of a farm fence. The paddock behind is private.
trees.story:
"This karri tree has engulfed another tree," wrote the reader who sent it to us from a gravel road west of Pemberton. "If you look carefully there is a birch like tree in its embrace."

Look at the photograph and you can find it. Up the middle of the great dark trunk runs a second, slimmer stem, paler and smoother, which the karri has grown around and swallowed for much of its height before both open into the crown. What the second tree is we cannot say from the picture; the reader saw birch in it, and Western Australia has no native birch, so tell us if you know.

The karri itself is unmistakable. Karri is one of the tallest hardwoods on earth and grows only in the wet southwest corner of Western Australia, around towns like Pemberton. This one stands almost alone on the verge, with a paddock behind it and the forest held back at the edge of the fields, so its crown has spread wide instead of tall. The reader measures the trunk at about six metres round, their figure and not one we have seen elsewhere.

Pull over on the red gravel and walk round the trunk to see where the two trees meet.

trees.name: The Twin Karri of Anzac Road

location.address: Beside Anzac Road, a forest track north-west of Pemberton, Western Australia

trees.how_to_recognise: In the forest by Anzac Road: two pale karri stems joined into one massive base, their smooth bark patched cream, grey and rust, splitting apart only high up where the branches begin.
trees.access: By a forest track west of Pemberton. We have not checked the track's condition; it may suit a high-clearance vehicle better than a car.
trees.story:
A reader sent us this karri from the forest beside Anzac Road, a track west of Pemberton, with a photograph that does the only thing you can do beside a karri, which is to look straight up.

What you see is two trees that grew as one. Two stems rise from a single massive base, pressed so close that their bark has fused into one surface, and they only part high above, where each opens into its own fan of pale limbs. The bark is the karri's own, smooth and shedding in patches, so the trunk is mottled cream, grey and rust from the ground to the crown. The reader measures the base at about five metres round, their figure.

Karri grows only in the wet southwest corner of Western Australia and is among the tallest hardwoods in the world, which is why the forests around Pemberton were felled hard for a century and why the town's lookout trees were karris. This one stands in the forest proper, among other tall trunks, and we do not know its height or age.

Stand at the base, between the two stems, and look up to where they finally separate.
